title: Japan September services PPI holds at 3.7% y/y, in line with forecast, before BoJ
body: An in-line print is unlikely to move the yen much on its own, but it removes one possible dovish surprise before Friday's decision and keeps the backdrop supportive of December hike pricing. Steady services inflation strengthens the case for the Outlook Report to effectively declare underlying inflation has reached 2%, which would support the yen and short-end JGB yields. The bigger moves are still likely to come from the BoJ's vote split, Ueda's press conference and Wednesday's Fed decision. Oil-driven cost pressure tied to the Iran conflict keeps the wider inflation backdrop firm. --- Earlier: BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk Japan services PPI preview: 3.7% pace in focus ahead of Friday's BoJ decision --- Japan's firms are still passing on service costs at a two-year-high pace, handing the BoJ one more piece of evidence for the 2% declaration markets expect this week.

title: Greer warns $3.4 billion EU loan to Airbus may breach US-EU aircraft trade truce Alt headlines:
body: This is a warning shot rather than an escalation, so the immediate market impact is likely confined to aerospace names, with Airbus and Boeing shares the most exposed to any shift in trade rhetoric. The bigger risk is that aircraft financing becomes a fresh front in US-EU trade tensions at a time when the administration is already fighting on several fronts, including Canada. Any move toward formal measures, such as reviving tariffs linked to the old subsidy dispute, would weigh on European aerospace and the wider supply chain. A quick EU response with loan details would likely defuse the issue. --- The Boeing-Airbus feud is back on Washington's radar, with Greer warning that Europe's record loan to Airbus could unpick a hard-won aircraft truce unless Brussels starts sharing details.

title: Australia CPI preview: banks see 1.0% core rise, above the RBA's 0.8% forecast
body: The Australian dollar and front-end yields are set up for a binary reaction. With implied hike odds already above half, a trimmed mean at or above 1.0% would push November pricing closer to fully priced and support the currency. A 0.9% or lower print could see that pricing unwind quickly. Oil is central to the headline story: the fuel spike reflects the global energy shock tied to the Iran conflict, so further gains in crude would keep headline inflation elevated into year-end. The services component matters most for the RBA, since broadening price pressure would undercut the argument that this is purely an imported energy shock. The release coincides with RBA officials appearing before Senate Estimates, adding to the event risk. --- Earlier: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac's Ellis says read the data calls --- Australia's core inflation is set to overshoot the RBA's own forecast for another quarter, and with the banks split down the middle, Wednesday's print may decide whether the Board hikes on Melbourne Cup Day.

title: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac's Ellis says read the data calls
body: For rates traders, the note argues against reading too much into tone shifts between the press conference and market-focused speeches, and in favour of the minutes and officials' data interpretations as the cleaner signal. The Governor describing the labour market as a little tight, plus staff's downbeat view of supply capacity, leans hawkish and supports pricing for further tightening rather than a pause. The coming fortnight is dense with event risk for the Australian dollar and front-end yields: the quarterly CPI lands alongside Senate Estimates testimony, followed by the November decision, the Statement on Monetary Policy and further speeches. With supply shocks driving inflation, including energy, a firm CPI would reinforce the hawkish read. --- Yesterday: RBA's Hunter says inflation job not done after four hikes, November rise in view --- The RBA has never been chattier, but Westpac's Luci Ellis says traders hunting for promises should listen instead to how it reads the data, because that is where the real signal lives.

title: ROADMAP: Morgan Stanley sees three catalysts ending the correction to ~7150, then S&P 500 to 8,000
body: Morgan Stanley's Wilson's framework gives traders a roadmap: a final flush toward 7,100 to 7,200, slightly below the 200-day moving average, would be consistent with his view rather than a breakdown of it. The quality factor breaking out suggests leadership stays defensive until his catalysts clear, while beaten-down early-cycle groups such as semiconductors carry the most rebound potential once they do. The liquidity call is the key one to watch: any signal from the Fed on slowing balance sheet growth further, or on tightening financial conditions, would matter more for his timeline than AI headlines. Oil-driven inflation that keeps the Fed on its hiking path is the main threat to a quick resolution. --- Earlier: Citadel Securities warns AI trade has little margin for error as three risks converge Goldman Sachs: AI buildout to add up to 50bp to US core PCE, but the boost is temporary --- Wilson says the worst of the correction has already happened beneath the surface, and once AI, the midterms and Fed liquidity clear, the index can catch up with an 8,000 year-end target.

title: BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk
body: A hold with an effective 2% declaration and a firm Ueda press conference would support the yen and pull December hike pricing forward, pushing short-end JGB yields higher. The asymmetric risk is the vote: if the two reflationist members switch from opposing a hike to calling for a cut, the dovish signal could outweigh the hawkish language and trigger yen selling. USD/JPY is also exposed to this week's Fed meeting. A surprise US hike that sent the pair sharply higher is the kind of emergency that, per the Nikkei report, could put a back-to-back BoJ move on the table. Oil-driven inflation pressure from the Iran conflict adds to the case for a firmer BoJ tone. --- Earlier: BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike BOJ to hold at 1.25%, but Ueda signals further hikes toward neutral Nikkei slips, bounces, as Iran oil fears weigh; ING sees BOJ holding at 1.25%, two hikes in 2027 Still to come: Japan services PPI preview: 3.7% pace in focus ahead of Friday's BoJ decision --- The BoJ is set to stand still on rates this week while moving a big step forward on rhetoric, unless two dovish dissenters steal the headlines and the yen pays for it.

title: ICYMI: Morgan Stanley sees 10%-15% more downside for Chinese offshore stocks before a bottom
body: The call sets a clear valuation marker: offshore Chinese shares near eight times forward earnings would be historically cheap territory, and that could become a reference point for bottom-fishing. Until then, Hong Kong-listed Chinese stocks look more exposed than mainland shares, which Morgan Stanley sees as cushioned by government support. The link to the global AI sell-off means Chinese equities are trading partly as a proxy for global risk appetite. Further weakness in US tech could spill over even without fresh domestic news. Any sign of policy support or clarity on the trust tax issue would be the obvious upside risk to the bearish view. --- Yesterday: Goldman Sachs cuts Kospi target 25% to 9,000, still sees over 60% upside --- Morgan Stanley thinks China's stock slide has another leg to go before valuations hit their historical floor, though it still sees Beijing's support making mainland shares the safer place to wait.
